title: Dot the I
full_review:
Here's a tale that's definitely not what it starts out to be. For the first hour of "Dot the I" (Summit Entertainment), you'd swear this was to be your typical romantic triangle story, though a downright seamy one at that.

The setting is London, and what you have is a temperamental flamenco dancer named (what else?) Carmen (Natalia Verbeke) who, recovering from an abusive relationship in her native Spain, agrees to marry Barnaby (James D'Arcy), a gentlemanly Brit who's a bit dull but at least kind to her.

At her bachelorette party, she is encouraged to follow a certain French tradition of kissing the man of her choice as a symbolic gesture of farewell to the single life. She chooses the good-looking, out-of-work Brazilian actor Kit (Gael Garcia Bernal), who's been sitting a few yards away, boldly shooting her with his video camera.

The kiss -- much to the amazement of the waiters and other patrons -- is long and lingering, and clearly she is smitten. Confused by her emotions, Carmen flees the restaurant.

Kit eventually tracks her down and after several initial rebuffs, Carmen succumbs to his charms. But still scarred from her previous experience, and doubly skittish because of a sense that she's being mysteriously stalked, she proceeds with the marriage to Barnaby.

From this point onward, the plot veers into something closer to Hitchcock territory, so we'll say no more.

Neat though some of the twists are, writer-director Matthew Parkhill's tale is fairly convoluted. The plot is improbable in the extreme, and the execution -- despite some clever touches -- feels semiamateurish, and not just because of the many interspersed scenes shot on hand-held digital video.

The volatile Carmen character is not terribly likable; she's angry much of the time and thinks nothing of flouting the law, as when she pulls a scam at a hotel to get a free meal. And Verbeke's heavily accented dialogue makes for stilted line readings.

Similarly, it takes a while to adjust to the sound of Bernal -- so prevalent on movie screens in both "The Motorcycle Diaries" and "Bad Education" -- speaking English for the first time. There is some awkward delivery, and some of his Latino charisma is diminished in this rather ordinary role. But he's more than adequate.

Tom Hardy and Charlie Cox are appropriately hateful as Kit's disreputable young cronies.

Though the overall milieu is quite unpleasant, Parkhill does score some points for casting light on the underlying voyeurism of reality television.

Wholesome Doris Day's "Perhaps, Perhaps, Perhaps" hit is used to good effect over the opening credits, but "Pillow Talk" this latest kinky release most definitely is not!

This film contains much rough and crude language, sexual situations, partial rear nudity, suicide with associated gore, and murder without retribution. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
